name: Ivan Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start with cello practice at eight, an hour of scales before my neighbours are fully awake. Three or four days a week I'm in a session at Northlight Studios, recording strings for film trailers, games and the odd pop record. Evenings I teach five private students in my flat, and the quartet rehearses on Sundays. The sessions pay the best, but the quartet is the reason I do any of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you love about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The waiting wears me out. You sit in a booth for forty minutes while the producer argues about a snare sound, then you have to play perfectly on the first take. What I love is the quartet, four people breathing together in a cold church hall. Nobody pays me enough for the quartet, and I'd never give it up, because it's the only part of my week that is fully mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the hype was always bigger than the thing. I'd probably post something smug in the union group chat, to be honest. Session players have been told for twenty years that sample libraries would finish us, and we're still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but I don't think I'd be untouched. The producers at Northlight already use software to tidy up timing, and a few trailer jobs have gone to sample libraries. In this world that just carries on slowly, maybe one less session a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing very different. I'd keep my three studio days, keep the five students, and keep paying my union dues. Maybe I'd finally put more of my savings into paying down the flat Tomas and I bought last year, since I wouldn't need it sitting there as an emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little bit annoyed that everyone spent years panicking for nothing. But it would feel like the ground I know is still under my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe one less session a month. What does that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About four hundred, give or take, on a good rate. That's real money but it's not frightening, because Tomas has his nursing salary and we've got well over six months put aside. If I lose one trailer session a month, I'll just take one more student on a Tuesday night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the studio you'd worry about, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, who does the music editing and timing fixes, maybe. Her job is exactly the kind of tidy-up work software nibbles at. She's sharp, though, and she's been there twelve years, so I'd guess she'd be fine.

say: I'd tell the **union chat** that the hype was always bigger than the real thing.
I'd point out that **sample libraries** were meant to finish session players twenty years ago, and didn't.
think: I'd be **relieved**, though the studio already uses software for timing fixes.
I'd expect to lose maybe **one session a month** to sample libraries and tidy-up software.
do: Keep **three studio days**, five private students and quartet rehearsals on Sundays exactly as they are.
Put more **savings** towards paying down the flat he bought with Tomas last year.
feel: **Calm**, with a little irritation that everyone spent years panicking over nothing.
S0.quote: If I lose one trailer session a month, I'll just take one more student on a Tuesday night.
fieldNote: Ivan's **security** comes from a mix of income: sessions, teaching, the quartet, and a partner on a nurse's salary.
He has already seen **small losses** to sample libraries, and treats them as the normal weather of session work.
He measures any loss in **students**: one lost session means one more Tuesday student.

steps.text: Keep three Northlight session days and all five private cello students
Pay extra off the flat mortgage instead of holding cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at work: this is theft. These systems learned from recordings we played on, and nobody asked us or paid us. I'd back the union campaign for consent and payment, and I'd say so online even if it annoys the producers who hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the trailer and game work goes first, and that's about forty per cent of my income. Producers will generate a string bed in ten minutes and only bring in a real player for a solo line. The teaching and the quartet would hold up, because those are about being in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that studios can't use our past recordings to train these tools. I'd take on three or four more students straight away, while parents still want a human teacher. I won't touch the AI tools myself. I don't want to help build the thing that replaces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, more than scared. It feels like someone walked into the studio and took the chair from under me while I was playing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the tools. Some players might use them to get more work. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm slow with technology, and I'm not ashamed of it. I can't learn a new piece of software every six months and still practise four hours a day. I'd rather fight for a fair rule than become the cellist who presses generate for a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the household money if forty per cent of your income goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas's nursing pay covers the mortgage, and my teaching covers my half of the bills. We'd stop the summer trip to his parents' coast house, maybe. With our savings we'd be fine for a long time, but I'd hate being the one who earns less.

say: I'd call it **theft** at work, because the tools learned from our recordings without consent.
I'd back the **union campaign** for consent and payment, even if it annoys producers who hire me.
think: I expect trailer and game sessions, about **forty per cent** of my income, to go first.
I think **teaching** and the quartet hold up, because they depend on being in the room.
do: Go to every **union meeting** and push for a ban on training with players' past recordings.
Take on three or four **more students** straight away while parents still want a human teacher.
feel: **Angry** more than scared, as if someone took his chair mid-performance.
Some **pride** at stake, because he'd hate to become the lower earner at home.
S1.quote: I'd rather fight for a fair rule than become the cellist who presses generate for a living.
fieldNote: Ivan's response is **political**, not technical: he refuses the tools on principle and because he's slow with them.
He sees clearly that **session income** is exposed while teaching and live playing are not.
Tomas's **nursing salary** and their savings are the quiet reason he can afford to dig in.

steps.text: Attend every musicians' union meeting and back the consent-and-payment campaign
Post publicly in support of rules against training on players' recordings
Add three or four new private cello students on weekday evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we were warned and nobody listened. I'd be at whatever protest the union called, holding a cello case. Publicly I'd keep saying live music can't be faked, because I believe that's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my studio work is gone within a year of 2028. Every trailer house would switch overnight, and they wouldn't even need Northlight's live room. The quartet and the teaching survive the first three years, but with robots coming around 2031, I honestly don't know what happens to teaching after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Tomas the first week and work out what we live on with no session income. I'd move my teaching up to fifteen students and ask the community music school about a salaried post. I'd also get the quartet playing more paid concerts and weddings, because people in a frightening time still want a real person playing at their wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Two years is nothing. I'd still be learning the score of a film that no longer needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned robots around 2031. Does that three-year gap matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters a lot, because it's the difference between the studio and the room. A computer can fake a cello recording in 2028, but a robot sitting in my teaching chair is a different thing. I'd use those three years to make the teaching and live work as solid as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, you're carrying us for a while, and I'm sorry. He'd laugh and tell me hospitals will need nurses whatever happens. Then I'd probably not sleep.

say: I'd say musicians **warned** everyone, and I'd join any **union protest** with my cello case.
I'd keep saying in public that **live music** can't be faked.
think: I expect my **studio work** to be gone within a year of 2028.
I see **teaching** and the quartet lasting until robots come, and after that I don't know.
do: Work out with Tomas in **week one** how they live with no session income.
Grow teaching to **fifteen students** and ask the community music school about a salaried post.
Book the quartet for more **paid concerts** and weddings.
feel: **Frightened** by how short two years is.
**Guilty** that Tomas would be carrying the household for a while.
S2.quote: A computer can fake a cello recording in 2028, but a robot sitting in my teaching chair is a different thing.
fieldNote: He expects to lose a **large share** of his income, which puts him at alarmed despite the savings.
The **three-year gap** before robots is the window he'd use to shore up teaching and live work.
He leans hard on **Tomas** and the union, not on new skills or tools.

steps.text: Join union protests against studios replacing session players
Grow private cello teaching from five to fifteen students
Apply for a salaried post at the community music school
Lean on Tomas's nursing salary to cover the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with more time to organise. I'd say the government has five years to put a law in place that protects performers and pays us for what was taken. That's long enough to do something if people push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the studio work still goes, just around 2030 instead of right away. The difference is I'd see it coming, so I wouldn't be caught with a calendar full of trailer sessions that vanish. And the teaching would have until about 2034 before robots are any kind of question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start shifting the balance: fewer studio days, more teaching, and I'd try for a part-time contract with the city orchestra's education programme. I'd keep pushing the union. I'd also stop putting extra money into the flat and keep a bigger cash cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frozen. It's like seeing a storm on the horizon when you're still at the harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep a bigger cash cushion. How big?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve months of my half of the bills, not six. That means skipping the new bow I've been saving for, which hurts, because it's a lovely French bow. I'd keep the old bow and the savings, because a good bow won't pay the mortgage in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the AI tools with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather spend those five years getting better at teaching children, because that's the part of me a machine has the hardest time copying.

say: I'd say the government has **five years** to pass a law that protects and pays performers.
I'd argue that's long enough if **people push** hard.
think: I think **studio work** still goes, around 2030 instead of right away.
I see **teaching** safe until about 2034, so the warning stops me being caught out.
do: Cut studio days and try for a **part-time contract** in the city orchestra's education programme.
Raise his cash **cushion** to twelve months and skip buying a new bow.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frozen, like seeing a storm from the harbour.
S3.quote: I'd keep the old bow and the savings, because a good bow won't pay the mortgage in 2031.
fieldNote: Five years turns his reaction from protest into **planning**, but he still expects to lose session income.
He refuses AI tools again and bets on **teaching children** as the hardest part to copy.
Giving up the **French bow** shows how seriously he takes it.

steps.text: Apply for part-time work in the city orchestra's education programme
Build cash savings to twelve months instead of buying a new bow
Keep campaigning with the union for a performers' protection law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly: a law on training data, funding for live music, and real support for musicians who need to change. I'd say that loudly, because ten years is also enough time for everyone to do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years takes me to thirty-seven, and that's a different life. I'd probably have a teaching post by then, maybe kids of my own. The studio work fades, but I'd have time to move away from it gently instead of being thrown out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time master's in music education in the first year, paid from savings, so I'd qualify to teach in schools. I'd keep doing sessions while they last. And I'd stay on the union's committee, because the rules get written in the first few years, not the last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, actually. Still a bit sad that recording might stop being something people pay a person to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a master's, when you said you're slow to take on new things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a school classroom isn't new to me in the way software is. My mum was a music teacher, and I've watched her do it my whole life. Going back to study at thirty is a change I understand, unlike learning software I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the warning time change what you'd say to younger players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell my students who want to do sessions to learn to teach and to play live as well. Don't build your whole life in the studio booth.

say: I'd demand a **training-data law**, live music funding and support for musicians changing careers.
I'd warn that **ten years** is also enough time for everyone to do nothing.
think: **Ten years** takes me to thirty-seven, likely with a teaching post and maybe children.
I expect studio work to **fade gently** rather than vanish overnight.
do: Start a **part-time master's** in music education in year one, paid from savings.
Keep doing **sessions** while they last and stay on the union's committee.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with some sadness that recording may stop being paid human work.
S4.quote: Going back to study at thirty is a change I understand, unlike learning software I'd hate.
fieldNote: The long warning lets Ivan pick a change he **understands**: school teaching, like his mother.
He still won't learn AI tools; his **resistance** is to software, not to change itself.
He thinks the **early years** of rule-making matter most.

steps.text: Start a part-time master's in music education, paid from savings
Keep taking trailer and game sessions while studios still book players
Stay on the union committee drafting rules for recorded music

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough time to retrain or for any law to pass. What would help is a clear rule that our recordings can't be used without consent and payment, and a fund to keep live music and teaching paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the quartet. I think about what happens to small live music if everyone's incomes fall. People stop buying concert tickets before they stop buying bread. I'd want the city to keep funding small concerts, because that's where young players learn.

headlineQuote: Nobody pays me enough for the quartet, and I'd never give it up, because it's the only part of my week that is fully mine.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old** session cellist who also teaches five students and plays in a string quartet.
He's **progressive**, a committed union member, and refuses to use AI tools on principle.
He expects **studio income** to be hit first and treats teaching and live playing as his safe ground.
With **savings** and his partner Tomas's nursing salary, he can afford to dig in and campaign.
Only the **ten-year** picture moves him to retrain, toward school teaching like his mother.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain or pass any law.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **consent-and-payment** rule for recordings, plus funding for live music and teaching.
